Oliver Twist was written by Charles Dickens and first published in 1838. Dickens had known hardship as a child himself, and he wrote this story to show the cruel way the poor were treated, and to argue that every child, however lowly, deserves kindness and care. The book helped change how people thought about poverty. This retelling shares Oliver's journey gently for young readers.

Oliver Twist was born in a grim workhouse, a hard place where the poorest people were sent to live. His mother died the moment he was born, and so Oliver came into the world an orphan, with no one at all to care for him. He was raised on too little food and too little kindness, among many other unwanted children.

image.note: A bleak Victorian workhouse; a tiny orphan boy among many; grey, hard, but the boy's face gentle

pages.text: The children in the workhouse were kept half starved, given only thin gruel and never enough of it. The men who ran the place were cruel and mean, and grew rich by feeding the poor as little as they could. Yet through it all, little Oliver stayed gentle and good, which is a great deal harder than it sounds when the whole world is unkind to you.

image.note: Rows of thin, hungry children eating watery gruel from bowls; well-fed masters looking on coldly; injustice

pages.text: One day, driven by terrible hunger, the boys drew lots, and it fell to Oliver to do a daring thing. After finishing his tiny portion, he walked up to the master, held out his empty bowl, and spoke the words that would become famous: "Please, sir, I want some more." The whole hall fell silent in shock at his boldness.

image.note: Small Oliver bravely holding up his empty bowl to a huge, astonished master; a hall of frozen, staring boys; iconic

pages.text: The masters were outraged that a workhouse boy would dare ask for more. As punishment, they decided to be rid of him, and sold him off to work for a grim undertaker. There poor Oliver was treated badly and bullied cruelly by an older boy, until at last, pushed beyond all bearing, he made up his mind to run away and seek a better life.

image.note: Oliver bullied and miserable in a gloomy undertaker's shop; then his face setting with resolve to escape

pages.text: Oliver ran away to the great city of London, walking for days, hungry, footsore and alone. On the very edge of the city, a sharp, grinning boy about his own age took notice of him. This boy, nicknamed the Artful Dodger, was friendly and quick, and offered the exhausted Oliver food and a place to stay with an old man he knew. Grateful, Oliver followed him.

image.note: A weary Oliver on a London road; a cheeky, sharp-eyed street boy greeting him; the city looming ahead

chapters.title: The Old Man and the Boys

pages.text: The Dodger led Oliver to a hidden den where an old man named Fagin lived with a whole gang of boys. They gave Oliver food and seemed merry and welcoming. But innocent Oliver did not understand what these boys really were. Fagin was a criminal, and he trained the boys to be pickpockets, to steal from people in the crowded streets.

image.note: A shadowy den; a sly old man, Fagin, surrounded by a gang of ragged boys; food and false warmth; hidden danger

pages.text: Not knowing this, Oliver went out with the boys, and was horrified to see the Dodger pick a gentleman's pocket. The Dodger fled, and poor innocent Oliver was seized and blamed for the crime he had not done. He was dragged before the law, terrified, an honest boy accused of being a thief, with no one in all the city to speak for him.

image.note: The Dodger picking a pocket and darting away; the wrong boy, Oliver, seized by a crowd crying "Stop, thief!"; unjust

pages.text: But fortune turned. The kindly old gentleman who had been robbed saw that gentle Oliver could not possibly be the thief, and took pity on him. He brought the sick, frightened boy into his own comfortable home, cared for him tenderly, and treated him with a kindness Oliver had never known in all his hard life. For the first time, Oliver was safe, warm and loved.

image.note: A warm, comfortable home; a kind old gentleman caring for a recovering Oliver; the boy safe and loved at last

pages.text: Oliver blossomed in that good home, and might have lived happily ever after. But Fagin's gang were afraid that Oliver, now among honest people, might reveal their crimes. And a far more frightening man was involved: a violent criminal named Sikes. The gang was determined to get the boy back into their clutches, whatever it took.

image.note: Oliver happy in his new home; but in the shadows, Fagin and the menacing Sikes plotting to seize him back; threat

pages.text: The gang caught Oliver again and dragged him back into their dark world, forcing him to help the brutal Sikes with a robbery. But there was one good heart among the criminals: a young woman named Nancy, who pitied Oliver and could not bear to see the innocent boy destroyed. In secret, and at great risk to herself, she resolved to help him.

image.note: Oliver seized and dragged back by the gang; a troubled young woman, Nancy, watching with pity and resolve

pages.text: Bravely, Nancy slipped away to meet Oliver's kind protectors in secret, and told them where the boy could be found and how to save him. It was a courageous and dangerous thing to do. Nancy risked everything for a boy who was not even her own, moved only by kindness, and her courage would prove to be Oliver's salvation, though it cost her dearly.

image.note: Nancy meeting Oliver's protectors secretly on dark steps, whispering urgently; brave, self-sacrificing; noble

pages.text: Thanks to Nancy's courage, Oliver was rescued at last, and the truth of his life finally came to light. It was discovered that Oliver was not a nobody after all, but the lost child of a good family, with relatives who had been searching for him. His true friends took him in for good, and the criminals who had preyed on him were caught and brought to justice.

image.note: The truth revealed; Oliver embraced by newfound family; the gang caught by the law; light after darkness

pages.text: And so Oliver, who had begun life as a friendless workhouse orphan, half starved and blamed for crimes he never did, came at last to a loving home and a happy life. Through all his suffering, he had never once let the world's cruelty turn him cruel. He had stayed good, and in the end, goodness and a few brave, kind hearts saw him safely through.

image.note: Oliver grown happy and loved in a warm family home, the hard days behind him; goodness rewarded; closing

pages.text: Oliver's story was written to open people's eyes to how badly the poor, and poor children most of all, were treated in those days. By making readers love gentle Oliver, the author made them care about all the real children who suffered as he did. A story, it turns out, can do more than entertain. It can make the world a little kinder.

image.note: A wide view: the warm home in the foreground, the grim old workhouse small and distant behind; change, compassion
